body_text: TWFG Announces Second Quarter 2026 Results August 5, 2026 PDF Version – Total Revenues increased 45.1% for the quarter over the prior year period to $87.5 million – – Organic Revenue Growth Rate* of 37.0% for the quarter – – Net income of $17.3 million and Net Income Margin of 19.7% for the quarter – – Adjusted EBITDA Margin* expanded 530 basis points to 30.4% – – Raising full-year 2026 guidance – THE WOODLANDS, Texas, Aug. 05, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- TWFG, Inc. (“TWFG”, the “Company” or “we”) (NASDAQ: TWFG), a high-growth insurance distribution company, today announced results for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026. Second Quarter 2026 Highlights Total revenues for the quarter increased 45.1% to $87.5 million, compared to $60.3 million in the prior year period Commission income for the quarter increased 47.8% to $80.6 million, compared to $54.6 million in the prior year period Net income for the quarter was $17.3 million, compared to $9.0 million in the prior year period, and net income margin for the quarter was 19.7% up from 14.9% in the prior year period Diluted Earnings Per Share for the quarter was $0.18 and Adjusted Diluted Earnings Per Share* for the quarter was $0.38 Total Written Premium for the quarter increased 26.6% to $569.9 million, compared to $450.3 million in the prior year period Organic Revenue Growth Rate* for the quarter was 37.0% Adjusted Net Income* for the quarter increased 76.1% from the prior year period to $20.3 million, and Adjusted Net Income Margin* for the quarter was 23.2% Adjusted EBITDA* increased 75.8% to $26.6 million, with Adjusted EBITDA Margin expanding 530 basis points to 30.4%, compared to 25.1% in the prior year period Approximately $42.9 million in cash was used to repurchase 2,252,349 shares under the Company's $50 million share repurchase authorization, leaving approximately $7.1 million available for future repurchases. *Organic Revenue Growth Rate, Adjusted Net Income, Adjusted Net Income Margin, Adjusted EBITDA, Adjusted EBITDA Margin, and Adjusted Diluted Earnings Per Share are non-GAAP measures. Reconciliations of Organic Revenue Growth Rate to total revenue growth rate, Adjusted Net Income and Adjusted EBITDA to net income, Adjusted Diluted Earnings Per Share to diluted earnings per share and Adjusted Free Cash Flow to cash flow from operating activities, the most directly comparable financial measures presented in accordance with GAAP, are outlined in the reconciliation table accompanying this release. “Our second quarter results demonstrate our focus on delivering double digit growth. Written premium grew 26.6% with revenue growth of 45.1%, and our Adjusted EBITDA Margin expanded to 30.4%. Growth was driven across our Agency-in-a-Box, Corporate Stores, and MGA programs, along with contributions from our recent acquisitions,” said Gordy Bunch, CEO. “Operationally, we remain focused on the fundamentals that drive sustainable, profitable growth, including disciplined producer recruiting, deepening carrier partnerships, and continued investment in our proprietary technology to improve agent productivity and provide the best client experience. Our MGA programs continue to scale efficiently, contributing to expanding margins across the enterprise.” Second Quarter 2026 Results During the quarter, industry conditions remained favorable for TWFG's distribution model even as personal auto pricing continued downward industry-wide and homeowners rate increases continued to moderate. TWFG's diversified distribution platform, combining independent agency operations, proprietary MGA programs, and technology-enabled systems, continued to convert favorable carrier economics into premium growth and margin expansion. For the second quarter, Total Written Premium increased 26.6% to $569.9 million, compared with $450.3 million in the same period of the prior year. Growth was primarily volume-led rather than rate driven, consistent with the moderating rate environment, and was supported by three key factors: (1) continued organic growth in the Agency-in-a-Box network, including increased policy count and strong client retention; (2) continued scaling of the Company’s MGA programs; and (3) contributions from new corporate store acquisitions. Consolidated written premium retention was 93% for the quarter, up from 89% in the prior year period, Consolidated written premium retention excluding takeout renewals from TWFG MGA FL, LLC (“MGA FL”), was approximately 88%. Total revenues increased 45.1% to $87.5 million, compared to $60.3 million in the same period in the prior year, outpacing written premium growth by nearly 20 percentage points. This spread reflects a structural mix shift towards a higher-commission-rate business: Key TWFG MGA programs carry commission rates above 20% versus approximately 12% for the core Agency-in-a-Box network, and now represents a substantially higher share of total commission income than of total written premium. Organic Revenues, which exclude contingent, non-policy fee, other income, and those revenues generated from recently acquired businesses, were $75.5 million for the quarter, an increase of $20.4 million from $55.1 million in the same period last year. The Organic Revenue Growth Rate of 37.0% was driven by structural tailwinds from the 2025 MGA FL Citizens** takeout policies renewing into the quarter where the prior period had very little commissions. Commission expense for the quarter increased 24.4% to $42.5 million, reflecting acquisitions and continued production growth, while growing meaningfully slower than commission income; a roughly 2,300 basis point spread reflecting favorable mix shift and earned revenue with no corresponding commission expense for takeout policies and acquired books of business. Salaries and employee benefits were $11.8 million, up 24.1% compared to $9.5 million in the same period in the prior year, primarily due to incremental headcount associated with the Company’s continued acquisition strategy, MGA Florida infrastructure build-out, and public company maturity. Other administrative expenses rose 59.0% to $8.6 million, primarily driven by our completed acquisitions and continued investments to support our growth initiatives. Net income for the quarter was $17.3 million, compared to $9.0 million in the same prior year period resulting in a net income margin of 19.7%, up from 14.9% last year. Adjusted Net Income increased 76.1% to $20.3 million, with an Adjusted Net Income Margin of 23.2% compared to 19.1% in the same period in the prior year. Adjusted EBITDA grew 75.8% to $26.6 million, reflecting strong operating leverage across the platform, the higher-margin profile of our MGA operations, and the contribution of recent acquisitions including APIA and corporate store additions. The Adjusted EBITDA Margin expanded to 30.4%, compared to 25.1% in the second quarter of 2025. Cash flow from operating activities was $9.8 million, compared to $9.6 million in the same period of the prior year. Adjusted Free Cash Flow was $3.6 million, compared to $2.9 million in the same period of the prior year, primarily driven by the increase in net income, decrease in tax distributions to members, with a slight offset due to the increase in purchase of property and equipment in the current period. **A Citizens takeout refers to the Citizens Property Insurance Corporation depopulation program in Florida, under which policies are transferred from the state-backed insurer to approved private insurance carriers. This program is designed to reduce Citizens’ policy count and increase private market participation. Liquidity and Capital Resources As of June 30, 2026, the Company had unrestricted cash and cash equivalents of $73.7 million. We had full unused capacity on our revolving credit facility of $50.0 million as of June 30, 2026. The total outstanding term notes payable balance was $3.0 million as of June 30, 2026. During the first quarter of 2026, the Company's Board of Directors authorized a share repurchase program of up to $50.0 million of the Company’s Class A common stock. The authorization reflects the Board’s confidence in TWFG’s long-term growth outlook, strong cash generation profile and disciplined capital allocation framework. As of June 30, 2026, the Company had repurchased approximately $43.3 million under the program, with approximately $7.1 million remaining available for future repurchases. The program does not obligate the Company to repurchase any specific number of shares and may be suspended or discontinued at any time. 2026 Acquisitions Update TWFG Insurance Services completed the acquisition of Fortress Insurance Services, an Iowa-based independent agency with five locations, effective May 1, 2026, complementing our previous Midwest additions. This transaction joins a broader roster of 2025–2026 corporate store and MGA acquisitions — including Loften Wells, Mears, McInnis, Angers & Litz, Alabama Insurance Agency, and APIA — that together contributed approximately $51.0 million of incremental written premium in the first half of 2026. Updated 2026 Outlook Based on year-to-date performance and current business trends, the Company is increasing its full-year 2026 financial outlook: Metric Previous Guidance Updated Guidance Organic Revenue Growth* 10-15% 13-17% Total Revenues $285-$300 million $300-$320 million Adjusted EBITDA Margin* 22-25% 23-27% The updated outlook reflects stronger-than-expected performance across the core businesses and subsequent acquisitions. The Company is unable to provide a reconciliation of Organic Revenue Growth or Adjusted EBITDA Margin guidance to the most directly comparable GAAP measures without unreasonable effort due to the inherent difficulty in forecasting the timing and magnitude of items that have not yet occurred. The Company believes any such difference would be immaterial. *For a definition of Organic Revenue Growth Rate and Adjusted EBITDA Margin, see “Non-GAAP Financial Measures” below. Non-GAAP Financial Measures and Key Performance Indicators Non-GAAP Financial Measures Organic Revenue, Organic Revenue Growth, Adjusted Net Income, Adjusted Net Income Margin, Adjusted Diluted Earnings Per Share, Adjusted EBITDA, Adjusted EBITDA Margin and Adjusted Free Cash Flow included in this release are not measures of financial performance in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles in the United States of America (“GAAP”) and should not be considered substitutes for GAAP measures, including revenues (for Organic Revenue and Organic Revenue Growth), net income (for Adjusted Net Income, Adjusted Net Income Margin, Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA Margin), diluted earnings per share (for Adjusted Diluted Earnings Per Share), and cash flow from operating activities (for Adjusted Free Cash Flow), which we consider to be the most directly comparable GAAP measures. These non-GAAP financial measures have limitations as analytical tools, and when assessing our operating performance, you should not consider these non-GAAP financial measures in isolation or as substitutes for revenues, net income, operating cash flow or other consolidated financial statement data prepared in accordance with GAAP. Other companies may calculate any or all of these non-GAAP financial measures differently than we do, limiting their usefulness as comparative measures. Organic Revenue. Organic Revenue is total revenue (the most directly comparable GAAP measure) for the relevant period, excluding contingent income, non-policy fee income, other income and those revenues generated from acquired businesses with over $0.5 million in annualized revenue that have not reached the twelve-month owned mark. Organic Revenue Growth. Organic Revenue Growth is the change in Organic Revenue period-to-period, with prior period results adjusted to include revenues that were excluded in the prior period because the relevant acquired businesses had not reached the twelve-month-owned milestone, but have reached the twelve-month owned milestone in the current period. We believe Organic Revenue Growth is an appropriate measure of operating performance because it eliminates the impact of acquisitions, which affects the comparability of results from period-to-period. Adjusted Net Income. Adjusted Net Income is a supplemental measure of our performance and is defined as Net Income (the most directly comparable GAAP measure) before amortization, non-recurring or non-operating income and expenses, including equity-based compensation, adjusted to assume a single class of stock (Class A) and assuming noncontrolling interests do not exist while excluding the impact of the sale of non-current assets. We believe Adjusted Net Income is a useful measure because it adjusts for the after-tax impact of significant one-time, non-recurring items and eliminates the impact of any transactions that do not directly affect what management considers to be our ongoing operating performance in the period. These adjustments generally eliminate the effects of certain items that may vary from company-to-company for reasons unrelated to overall operating performance. Beginning in the year ended December 31, 2025, we updated our definition of Adjusted Net Income to exclude the impact of the sale of non-current assets. The impact of this change on our Adjusted Net Income for the year ended December 31, 2025, as well as on previously reported periods, was not material. As a result, prior‑period amounts have not been recast. We believe this minor refinement to our definition provides improved alignment with how management evaluates operating performance and enhances the measure’s usefulness for investors while maintaining comparability with prior periods. We are subject to U.S. federal income taxes, in addition to state, and local taxes, with respect to our allocable share of any net taxable income of TWFG Holding Company, LLC. Adjusted Net Income pre-IPO did not reflect adjustments for income taxes since TWFG Holding Company, LLC is a limited liability company and is classified as a partnership for U.S. federal income tax purposes. Post-IPO, the calculation incorporates the impact of federal and state statutory tax rates on 100% of our adjusted pre-tax income as if the Company owned 100% of TWFG Holding Company, LLC. Adjusted Net Income Margin. Adjusted Net Income Margin is Adjusted Net Income divided by total revenues. We believe that Adjusted Net Income Margin is a useful measurement of operating profitability for the same reasons we find Adjusted Net Income useful and also because it provides a period-to-period comparison of our after-tax operating performance. Adjusted Diluted Earnings Per Share. Adjusted Diluted Earnings Per Share is Adjusted Net Income divided by diluted shares outstanding after adjusting for the effect of (i) the exchange of 100% of the outstanding Class B common stock of the Company (the “Class B Common Stock”) and Class C common stock of the Company (the “Class C Common Stock”) (together with the related limited liability units in TWFG Holding Company, LLC (the “LLC Units”)) into shares of Class A common stock of the Company (“Class A Common Stock”) and (ii) the vesting of 100% of the unvested equity awards and exchange into shares of Class A Common Stock. This measure does not deduct earnings related to the noncontrolling interests in TWFG Holding Company, LLC for the period prior to July 19, 2024, when we did not own 100% of the business. The most directly comparable GAAP financial metric is diluted earnings per share. We believe Adjusted Diluted Earnings Per Share may be useful to an investor in evaluating our operating performance and efficiency because this measure is widely used by investors to measure a company’s operating performance without regard to items excluded from the calculation of such measure, which can vary substantially from company to company depending upon acquisition activity and capital structure. This measure also eliminates the impact of expenses that do not relate to core business performance, among other factors. Adjusted EBITDA. Adjusted EBITDA is a supplemental measure of our performance and is defined as EBITDA adjusted to reflect items such as equity-based compensation, interest income, other non-operating and certain nonrecurring items, while excluding the impact of the sale of non-current assets. EBITDA is defined as net income (the most directly comparable GAAP measure) before interest, income taxes, depreciation and amortization. We believe that Adjusted EBITDA is an appropriate measure of operating performance because it adjusts for significant one-time, non-recurring items and eliminates the ongoing accounting effects of certain capital spending and acquisitions, such as depreciation and amortization, that do not directly affect what management considers to be our ongoing operating performance in the period. These adjustments eliminate the effects of certain items that may vary from company to company for reasons unrelated to overall operating performance. Our measure of Adjusted EBITDA is not necessarily comparable to other similarly titled captions of other companies due to potential inconsistencies in the methods of calculation. Beginning in the year ended December 31, 2025, we updated our definition of Adjusted EBITDA to exclude the impact of the sale of non-current assets. The impact of this change on our Adjusted EBITDA for the year ended December 31, 2025, as well as on previously reported periods, was not material. As a result, prior‑period amounts have not been recast. We believe this minor refinement to our definition provides improved alignment with how management evaluates operating performance and enhances the measure’s usefulness for investors while maintaining comparability with prior periods. Adjusted EBITDA Margin. Adjusted EBITDA Margin is Adjusted EBITDA divided by total revenue. We believe that Adjusted EBITDA Margin is a useful measurement of operating profitability for the same reasons we find Adjusted EBITDA useful and also because it provides a period-to-period comparison of our operating performance. Adjusted Free Cash Flow. Adjusted Free Cash Flow is a supplemental measure of our performance. We define Adjusted Free Cash Flow as cash flow from operating activities (the most directly comparable GAAP measure) less cash payments for tax distributions, purchases of property, plant, and equipment and acquisition-related costs. We believe Adjusted Free Cash Flow is a useful measure of operating performance because it represents the cash flow from the business that is within our discretion to direct to activities including investments, debt repayment, and returning capital to stockholders. The reconciliation of the above non-GAAP measures to their most comparable GAAP financial measure is outlined in the reconciliation table accompanying this release. Key Performance Indicators Total Written Premium. Total Written Premium represents, for any reported period, the total amount of current premium (net of cancellations) placed with insurance carriers. We utilize Total Written Premium as a key performance indicator when planning, monitoring, and evaluating our performance. We believe Total Written Premium is a useful metric because it is the underlying driver of the majority of our revenue. title: Illinois American Water Recognizes Parent Company American Water's 140 Years of Providing Safe and Reliable Water and Wastewater Services to Customers and Communities in 2026
summary: Illinois American Water, a subsidiary of American Water, the largest regulated water and wastewater utility in the U.S., proudly highlights American Water's 140-year milestone of providing safe,...
body_text: BELLEVILLE, Ill. , Aug. 6, 2026 / PRNewswire / -- Illinois American Water, a subsidiary of American Water, the largest regulated water and wastewater utility in the U.S., proudly highlights American Water's 140-year milestone of providing safe, clean, reliable, and affordable water and wastewater services to the communities it serves. Founded in 1886, American Water now serves more than 14 million people across 14 regulated states and 19 military installations, including 1.3 million people in Illinois. "Illinois American Water remains committed to investing in the systems and communities who rely on us every day," said Rebecca Losli, President, Illinois American Water. "As our parent company celebrates 140 years of providing safe, reliable water and wastewater service in 2026, we are proud to continue that legacy locally. In Illinois, we plan to invest approximately $570 million in infrastructure upgrades through 2027, to further enhance reliability and system resiliency for our customers." Additionally, Illinois American Water will recognize the following milestones in 2026, including: The 30 th anniversary of Illinois American Water's H2O Help to Others™ Program, assisting customers who would otherwise have trouble paying their bills with supplemental funding. Since 2020, Illinois American Water has assisted more than 11,000 customers. 54 years of membership with the American Water Works Association and Partnership for Safe Water (1972) , collaborating to protect water systems and infrastructure. The 15 th anniversary of the American Water Charitable Foundation , commemorating more than $25 million in funding through grants and matching gifts to communities served by American Water. In 2025, the American Water Charitable Foundation and Illinois American Water employees contributed more than $400,000 to 270 organizations throughout Illinois. In 2026 to date, 14 organizations were recognized as Water & Environment grant recipients, and applications are currently being accepted for the 2026 Hydration Station Grant Program . The 45 th anniversary of American Water's Research & Development Program , advancing science and innovation to support the long‑term safety and reliability of drinking water systems. This includes the company's Central Laboratory in Belleville, IL, which runs 36 standard test methods for more than 260 compounds. In 2025 the lab ran an average of 273 tests per day. The analytical strength of American Water across our service footprint allows us to be a leader in developing solutions, including our collaboration to develop a response plan in the event of harmful algal blooms. Learn more about American Water's history here . About American Water American Water (NYSE: AWK) is the largest regulated water and wastewater utility company in the United States. With a history dating back to 1886 and celebrating 140 years in 2026, We Keep Life Flowing® by providing safe, clean, reliable and affordable drinking water and wastewater services to approximately 14 million people with regulated operations in 14 states and on 19 military installations. American Water's approximately 7,000 talented professionals leverage their significant expertise and the company's national size and scale to achieve excellent outcomes for the benefit of customers, employees, investors and other stakeholders. For more information, visit amwater.com and join American Water on LinkedIn , Facebook , X and Instagram . About Illinois American Water Illinois American Water, a subsidiary of American Water, is the largest regulated water utility in the state with approximately 600 dedicated employees working to provide safe, clean, reliable and affordable water and wastewater services to approximately 1.3 million people. American Water also operates a quality control and research laboratory in Belleville. SOURCE American Water

body_text: Vishay Intertechnology TSOP15300 Series IR Receivers Support All Major Remote Control Codes August 4, 2026 PDF Version Saving Space and Reducing Component Counts to Simplify Universal Remote Control Designs, Devices Feature a Wide 30 kHz to 68 kHz Modulation Frequency Range MALVERN, Pa., Aug. 04, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Vishay Intertechnology, Inc. (NYSE: VSH) today introduced a new series of infrared (IR) receiver modules for IR remote control applications. Featuring a wide modulation frequency acceptance from 30 kHz to 68 kHz, devices in the Vishay Semiconductors TSOP15300 series are designed to receive and demodulate all major remote control codes on the market, enabling a single-component universal remote control solution. Standard IR receivers are typically tuned to one center frequency, limiting compatibility and requiring multiple devices to cover different code sets. With their wide modulation frequency range, the receivers released today overcome this limitation, reducing component counts to lower system costs and save board space. Designed for consumer electronics such as televisions, audio systems, gaming consoles, soundbars, set-top boxes (STB), video projectors, and more, TSOP15300 series receivers provide immunity against ripple noise and interference from common sources like IR emissions in CFL lamps and LCD televisions, and RF emissions from onboard Wi-Fi antennas. When paired with a 50 mA emitter, the devices offer reliable transmission distances of up to 18 m. To simplify designs, each receiver integrates a photodetector, preamplifier circuit, and IR filter within a 4-pin Heimdall package. For decoding, their demodulated output signal can be directly connected to a microprocessor. Optimized for short burst codes, TSOP15300 series devices operate over a wide supply voltage range from 2.0 V to 5.5 V, draw a typical supply current of 0.35 mA, and feature a maximum irradiance of 0.2 mW/m² at 45 kHz. They are RoHS-compliant, halogen-free, and Vishay Green . Samples and production quantities of the new IR receiver modules are available now, with lead times of six weeks. Vishay manufactures one of the world’s largest portfolios of discrete semiconductors and passive electronic components that are essential to innovative designs in the automotive, industrial, computing, consumer, telecommunications, military, aerospace, and medical markets. body_text: PDF Version OLD GREENWICH, Conn.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aug. 12, 2026-- Ellington Credit Company (NYSE: EARN) ("we") today reported financial results for the quarter ended June 30, 2026. Highlights Net asset value (NAV) per share was $4.18 as of June 30, 2026, which includes the effects of distributions of $0.24 per share for the quarter. GAAP net income was $12.3 million, or $0.33 per share. Net investment income ("NII") was $6.1 million, or $0.16 per share. Adjusted net investment income1 was $5.7 million, or $0.15 per share. CLO portfolio was $334.1 million as of June 30, 2026. CLO debt investments—$154.1 million CLO equity investments—$180.0 million Purchased $64.8 million of CLO investments and sold $35.1 million, across 64 trades. Weighted average GAAP yield2 for the quarter, based on amortized cost, was 11.9% on the total CLO portfolio. Received $17.6 million in recurring cash distributions3 from the CLO portfolio, or $0.47 per share. Raised $2.6 million through the issuance4 of 579,416 common shares prices representing a 5% weighted average premium to NAV per share. Management Commentary "The second calendar quarter validated the actions we took in response to the first quarter market dislocation," said Laurence Penn, Chief Executive Officer and President. "The market selloff early in the year enhanced the CLO opportunity set, and we responded by rapidly deploying the proceeds from our March unsecured note offering while actively repositioning the portfolio. Although net investment income for the quarter did not yet fully reflect our expanded and repositioned portfolio, we generated a quarterly economic return of 8% (non-annualized), grew NAV per share, and enhanced our future earnings capacity. "As market conditions stabilized during the quarter, we refined our portfolio to upgrade credit quality and improve long-term return potential. In mezzanine debt, we rotated out of lower-coupon, shorter-spread-duration positions trading near or above par and into higher-coupon, wider-spread investments with stronger underlying credit fundamentals. In CLO equity, we added longer-tenor, higher-cash-flow structures while reducing exposure to shorter-tenor positions with greater sensitivity to loan price volatility. We also benefited from several refinancings and resets of existing CLO equity positions, enhancing both near-term cash flows and long-term earnings power. "Looking ahead, we believe that the market dynamics that emerged during the second quarter — including higher reinvestment yields, improving credit fundamentals, and a more constructive technical backdrop — continue to favor active portfolio management. We expect net investment income to grow as we deploy the excess liquidity held at quarter end, selectively increase leverage, and rotate the portfolio toward higher-yielding investments. Combined with our active trading capabilities, flexible balance sheet, and disciplined hedging strategy, EARN is well positioned to generate attractive risk-adjusted returns for our shareholders." ____________________ 1 Adjusted net investment income is a non-GAAP financial measure. CLO Performance During the quarter ended June 30, 2026, the leveraged loan and broader corporate credit markets improved significantly. Easing geopolitical tensions, improving investor sentiment, and reduced default concerns in the software sector supported a sharp tightening in credit spreads. This, in turn, contributed to a meaningful increase in new issue supply across investment grade, high yield, and leveraged loan markets as borrowers sought to capitalize on improving market conditions to raise new financing. Despite weakness in June due to elevated loan issuance and quarter-end selling pressures, the Morningstar LSTA US Leveraged Loan Index rose by $0.33 during the quarter, while the European leveraged loan market generally outperformed the U.S. market, driven in part by more limited new-issue supply. Improving loan market conditions supported strong performance across both mezzanine debt and CLO equity during the quarter. At quarter-end, the balance of loans in CLOs trading below $80 (a common proxy for distress) had declined by nearly a full percentage point to 5.4%. The recovery in several stressed credits reduced some concerns around future collateral losses, while refinancings of shorter-term loans trading at discounts to par further strengthened the overall credit quality of many underlying loan portfolios. Meanwhile, slowing repricing activity, particularly among premium-priced loans, moderated the compression of excess spreads, alleviating a recent headwind for CLO equity. Increased primary loan issuance also created attractive opportunities for CLO managers to reinvest principal proceeds into new, wider-spread loans, supporting future cash flows and long-term earnings power. Together, these developments created a favorable environment for CLO equity and lower-quality seasoned mezzanine debt. Higher-quality mezzanine tranches, already trading near par, offered more limited upside. Our investment portfolio generated excellent results for the quarter, driven by net investment income as well as net realized and unrealized gains across U.S. equity and U.S. and European mezzanine investments. We also benefited from trading gains on mezzanine debt, and gains from the call of discounted mezzanine debt positions. Net losses on our credit hedges partially offset these gains. At June 30, 2026, our CLO portfolio had a fair value of $334.1 million and a weighted average projected yield of 16.6% (based on fair value), and we held cash and cash equivalents of $23.5 million. The Fund is externally managed and advised by an affiliate of Ellington Management Group, L.L.C., a leading fixed-income investment manager founded in 1994. title: Can You Learn Spanish in 3 Months? Fluency Levels to Expect
summary: Three months is a realistic window to reach conversational Spanish, but only if the approach matches the goal. Most learners lose time on grammar-heavy methods…
body_text: Three months is a realistic window to reach conversational Spanish, but only if the approach matches the goal. Most learners lose time on grammar-heavy methods that rarely translate to actual speaking ability. Understanding what 90 days can genuinely deliver, and how to structure each week, makes the difference between functional conversation and frustrating stagnation. Focused, spoken practice accelerates progress far more than traditional study. Parrot is built around exactly that, prioritizing real conversation over drills so learners build vocabulary, pronunciation, and confidence at the same time. Anyone serious about the best way to learn conversational Spanish should learn Spanish with a tool designed for that specific outcome. Table of Contents Can You Really Learn Spanish in 3 Months? What Research Says About Learning Spanish in Three Months What Determines How Much Progress You Make in 90 Days A Practical 90-Day Plan for Learning Spanish Is Three Months the Right Goal for You? How Parrot Helps You Make the Most of 90 Days Start Learning Spanish Today Summary Reaching conversational Spanish at an A2 to B1 level in 90 days is possible, but it requires roughly 20 hours of study per week according to Speakeasy BCN. That is closer to a part-time job than most learners expect, and the gap between that standard and casual daily study (which typically produces only 90 to 120 hours over three months) explains why so many people feel like they underperformed when they were simply under-informed about the math. Consistency produces better results than intensity at every stage of language acquisition. Distributed practice across short, daily sessions builds stronger long-term retention than the same total hours compressed into occasional marathons. Research on second language acquisition consistently shows that the learner who shows up for 15 minutes every day will outperform the one who studies hard for two weeks and then stops, because memory consolidation happens in the gaps between sessions, not during them. The method matters more than the time spent. Comprehensible input, Spanish that is mostly understandable while still introducing unfamiliar structures, accelerates vocabulary and grammar acquisition in ways that isolated drills and flashcard decks cannot replicate. When the brain is decoding meaning rather than memorizing rules, it absorbs patterns through repeated exposure to real communication, which is the mechanism behind Dr. Stephen Krashen's comprehensible input theory. Most learners underestimate the gap between passive recognition and active speech. Reading and listening build a passive vocabulary that does not automatically transfer to spoken output. Speaking from the beginning, even imperfectly, trains the retrieval system alongside the storage system, and shadowing native speakers builds both ear and mouth at the same time. Delaying speaking until you "feel ready" is one of the most common reasons learners plateau around weeks five and six. Goals framed around a 90-day window are associated with higher completion rates than annual goals, according to Mooncamp's goal-setting research. The three-month horizon is close enough to feel urgent and concrete enough to plan around, but it only works when the target is accurately defined. Aiming for conversational confidence rather than native-level fluency sets a realistic benchmark and prevents the early dropout that comes from measuring progress against the wrong standard. Authentic listening practice closes a gap that structured lesson audio never can. Textbook recordings are slow and carefully enunciated, while real Spanish compresses syllables, blends words, and shifts rhythm in ways that only daily exposure to natural speech can prepare you for. Even 15 minutes of real Spanish content daily builds familiarity with connected speech in ways that compound quietly over weeks. Parrot's Learn Spanish addresses this by delivering short-form authentic video with comprehensible input and spaced repetition, so daily immersion feels like watching content rather than grinding exercises. Can You Really Learn Spanish in 3 Months? Three months is enough time to make real , measurable progress in Spanish. Whether that progress counts as "learning Spanish" depends entirely on what you mean by those words. " Three months of focused effort can take a learner from zero to a genuinely functional level in Spanish: the definition of 'learning' is everything." 🎯 Key Point: The question isn't whether you can learn Spanish in 3 months —it's what level of Spanish you're aiming for. Being able to have a conversation — talking back and forth with native speakers without a script — takes longer than 90 days for most people. According to Speakeasy BCN , Spanish can reach conversational level (A2–B1) in about 3 months with 20 hours per week of intensive study . That's a meaningful goal, but most learners aren't starting from that position. Casual Hours Per Week 3–5 hours Realistic Outcome in 3 Months Basic phrases and survival vocabulary Moderate Hours Per Week 10–12 hours Realistic Outcome in 3 Months A1–A2 proficiency with simple conversations Intensive Hours Per Week 20+ hours Realistic Outcome in 3 Months A2–B1 proficiency with conversational ability ⚠️ Warning: 20 hours per week is not a casual commitment — that's nearly 3 hours every single day . Most learners significantly overestimate how much time they'll actually put in. What three months can give you is something genuinely useful : a working vocabulary , enough listening comprehension to follow slow, clear speech , and the ability to handle practical situations like ordering food, asking for directions, or introducing yourself. For a traveler or someone preparing for a new role , that level of ability transforms the experience completely . 🔑 Takeaway: Three months won't make you fluent , but it will make you functional . For many real-world goals, functional is enough . Why does the word "fluency" create so much confusion? The confusion starts with the word "fluency," which describes everything from basic survival phrases to near-native proficiency . When someone claims they "learned Spanish in 90 days," they rarely specify which version they mean. The claim isn't always wrong—just incomplete. Most learners underestimate the gap between recognizing language and producing it. You can read menus, follow slow podcasts, or recognize repeated words and still freeze when someone speaks at natural speed. Recognition and production are different skills , and three months of passive study builds the first without reliably building the second. Does your method matter more than how much time you spend? The method matters more than the timeline. A learner spending 10 minutes daily with comprehensible input—content slightly above their current level but understandable in context—will outpace someone grinding grammar exercises for an hour. This is Dr. Stephen Krashen's core insight: language is acquired through understanding messages , not memorizing rules. The brain learns to speak by processing meaning repeatedly in context, not by studying conjugation tables. Most Spanish apps treat language as a subject to study rather than a skill to absorb, rewarding streaks and gamifying drills that feel productive but rarely translate into real conversation. Parrot's Learn Spanish works differently, using short-form video and spaced repetition to deliver daily immersive listening and speaking practice: the kind of input that builds conversational ability rather than quiz scores. What should you realistically expect after three months of consistent practice? Consistency beats intensity. Ten to fifteen minutes of daily immersion compounds faster than a 30-minute weekly session. The learner who shows up every day for three months will outperform one who studies hard for two weeks and then stops. The honest timeline for conversational fluency sits closer to 6 to 12 months for most learners using a sound method. After three months, you should hold simple conversations, understand common phrases at moderate speed, and feel comfortable in everyday situations—a meaningful milestone. A common pattern among learners who quit early is setting the wrong goal. They aimed for fluency in 90 days, hit month two still stumbling through basic sentences, and concluded they weren't "language people." The problem was never their ability, but the mismatch between goal, method, and timeline. What Research Says About Learning Spanish in Three Months How you practice Spanish matters more than how much time you spend on it. According to Speakeasy BCN , reaching B2 level requires 600 to 750 hours of study under the Common European Framework of Reference . Three months of casual daily study typically gives you only 90 to 120 hours of actual exposure — a gap that's a math problem you can fix , not a sign that you can't learn Spanish. "Reaching B2 level requires 600 to 750 hours of study under the Common European Framework of Reference ." — Speakeasy BCN Casual Daily Study Hours in 3 Months 90–120 hours Gap to B2 Approximately 480–660 hours remaining Intensive Daily Study Hours in 3 Months 300–400 hours Gap to B2 Approximately 200–450 hours remaining Full Immersion Program Hours in 3 Months 500–600 hours Gap to B2 Approximately 0–250 hours remaining 🔑 Takeaway: The 600–750 hour benchmark isn't meant to discourage you — it reveals exactly where the leverage is. Close the hours gap with higher-quality, intentional practice, and you dramatically change what's possible in three months . 💡 Tip: Instead of asking "how long should I study?" ask "how can I make every hour count more?" — active recall , real conversation practice , and spaced repetition can multiply the value of every hour you put in. ⚠️ Warning: Most learners underestimate the hours required and overestimate the impact of passive exposure like background TV or music. Intentional, active study is what moves the needle. Does study quality matter more than study hours? The failure point is usually a mismatch between study hours and study quality. Research on second language acquisition shows that comprehensible input —Spanish you can mostly understand while encountering unfamiliar words—drives faster vocabulary growth than grammar drills or isolated memorization. A learner spending 30 minutes daily with authentic Spanish content they can follow builds fundamentally different skills than someone using flashcard decks for the same duration. One approach trains your brain to process Spanish as communication; the other trains it to recognize patterns in isolation. Why does consistency beat intensity for language retention? The same research shows that regular practice beats intense cramming. Practicing in short, frequent sessions helps you retain information better than studying the same total hours in a few long sessions. Most learners break this pattern: they study hard for a week, miss four days, then quit. That cycle works against how language learning actually sticks in your brain. Apps like Parrot are built around this idea, using comprehensible language in short daily sessions with spaced repetition to help you stay consistent. How much progress is actually achievable? Progress depends on hours invested. Speakeasy BCN reports that 20 hours per week of intensive Spanish study can allow learners to complete one to two CEFR levels in three months, yielding gains in listening comprehension, vocabulary range, and conversational ability. Half that commitment, applied consistently with quality input, produces noticeably different results at the 90-day mark compared to the same hours spent on memorization and repetition. What does real progress look like at the 90-day mark? Three months is enough time to build a foundation where familiar conversations no longer require mental translation , where you catch meaning before thinking about every word. This is not fluency, but the moment when Spanish starts to feel less like a subject and more like a skill within reach with the right method applied consistently. The deeper question is not whether three months is enough time, but what determines how much of that time becomes real progress. One can hold simple conversations with confidence. The other gets nervous when a native speaker talks faster . The gap between them is never about talent or dedication : it's about how they spent their time . "The gap between learners after 90 days is never about talent or dedication : it's about how they spent their time ." 🎯 Key Point: Equal time investment does not guarantee equal results . The quality and structure of your study sessions matter far more than the hours logged . 🔑 Takeaway: If you want to hold real conversations after 90 days , the most critical variable isn't how long you study: it's what you do during every single session. Daily consistency is the real multiplier The failure point is usually invisible: learners assume that more hours in a single session compensate for days of absence. A 20-minute daily session works better than a three-hour Saturday study block because your brain solidifies language during the gaps between exposures. Repetition across days builds the neural pathways that make recall feel automatic rather than effortful. Serious learners often discover this the hard way. After weeks of inconsistent study, vocabulary they "learned" disappears, requiring relearning. Consistency is not a discipline hack; it is how memory works. What kind of input you consume matters more than how much The quality of what you learn matters more than how often you learn it. Comprehensible input—Spanish that you can mostly understand while learning new structures—helps you learn faster than grammar drills and isolated vocabulary lists. When your brain figures out meaning rather than memorizing rules, it picks up patterns naturally, the way children learn language by hearing real messages repeatedly. Why do most learners hit a wall with apps and drills? Most learners default to popular apps or first-search courses, grinding through levels and collecting streaks like a game. Around week four or five, gamified drills stop feeling like progress and start feeling like a treadmill. Apps built on comprehensible input methodology, like Parrot , use short-form video and spaced repetition to sustain daily immersion tied to real conversational patterns rather than synthetic exercises. The gap between passive knowledge and active speech Learners who delay speaking often find themselves understanding more than they can say. Passive vocabulary built through reading or listening does not automatically transfer to spoken output. Retrieving words under the pressure of real conversation is a different cognitive task. Speaking from the beginning trains the retrieval system alongside storage. Shadowing native speakers, narrating moments out loud, or working with a conversation partner even once a week gives your brain practice pulling words out, not putting them in. That distinction matters more over 90 days than most learners expect. Listening to authentic Spanish daily closes the real-world gap Lesson audio is clean, slow, and carefully spoken. Real Spanish is none of those things. Native speakers compress syllables, blend words together, and shift rhythm in ways that no textbook prepares you for. Learners who limit themselves to lesson audio often hit a wall when encountering an actual conversation , a podcast, or a television show. Why does even 15 minutes of authentic audio compound over time? According to Asian Efficiency , successful people use 90-day planning periods to measure progress. Fifteen minutes of Spanish daily—whether a short video, conversation clip, or podcast segment at your level—builds familiarity with natural rhythm and connected speech that compounds over weeks. Vocabulary learned in context sticks; vocabulary memorized in lists fades Learners who rely on word lists can recognize vocabulary in isolation but cannot recall it when needed in sentences. Context is how your brain remembers words. When you encounter a word in a story, video, or conversation, your brain stores not just the meaning but also the situation, feeling, and surrounding words. That contextual memory lets you retrieve a word quickly during conversation instead of searching for it while others continue talking. Motivation is not a personality trait; it is a design problem Students who enjoy what they are learning stay consistent. Students who treat every session like a chore find reasons to skip it. This is not about willpower; it is about whether the content makes Spanish feel alive rather than assigned. Why does engaging content keep the daily habit alive? Watching a cooking channel, following a travel creator, or listening to a sports podcast in Spanish does what a textbook cannot: it makes the language feel worth understanding. That emotional pull sustains the daily habit past the first two weeks, when novelty fades, and discipline alone rarely holds. What separates learners who make the most of three months? Matt Gray on LinkedIn documented achieving three years of progress in 90 days using a focused planning framework. Learners who gain the most from three months aren't those who study hardest in single sessions, but those who build a structure they can sustain: engaging content, short daily sessions, and habits that reinforce each other. Knowing what drives progress is one thing. Arranging those habits into a workable plan is where most learners get stuck. Sequence your habits so they build on each other rather than work against each other. Weeks 1 to 4 Build What You Can Actually Use Start with high-frequency vocabulary: greetings, common verbs , numbers, food, directions, and daily routines. These words appear repeatedly in real content, so each hour spent learning them pays dividends for months. How much grammar do you actually need in the first month? Pair vocabulary work with enough grammar to make simple sentences: present-tense verbs, basic sentence structure, question formation . The goal isn't to master everything but to recognize patterns. You want to understand how a sentence is built even when you don't know some of the words. Why should you train your ear from day one? Train your ear to recognize Spanish at natural speed from day one. Connected speech transforms from an impenetrable wall into a recognizable pattern. According to the Berlitz Blog , spending at least 30 minutes daily practicing Spanish can yield noticeable progress within 90 days. What matters most is how you spend those 30 minutes: passive review rarely builds the brain pathways that active, meaning-focused engagement does. Weeks 5 to 8: Let the Language Come to You Most 90-day plans fail around week five. Learners finish their beginner course, know a few hundred words, then encounter real Spanish and understand almost nothing. That gap feels like failure. It isn't. It's the exact moment where real learning begins. Why does comprehensible input become your primary tool at this stage? This is when comprehensible input becomes your primary tool. Beginner-friendly video content, slow Spanish podcasts, and graded readers pitched above your current level won't be fully understood—and that's the point. The brain acquires language by decoding meaning, not by achieving perfect comprehension. Repeated exposure to near-comprehensible material is where vocabulary and grammar stick without deliberate memorization. A common plateau pattern occurs when learners focus heavily on reading or structured study without balancing listening. This creates a separate gap requiring later effort to close, particularly with unfamiliar accents or connected speech. Building both skills in parallel during this phase prevents the problem from worsening. When should you start speaking and how does it accelerate progress? This is where speaking starts—not when you feel ready, but now. Short self-talk sessions, basic language exchanges, and simple descriptions of your day transform passive recognition into active retrieval, a different cognitive skill entirely. Shadowing, where you repeat phrases immediately after hearing them, bridges the two by training your ear and mouth simultaneously. Most learners default to structured study apps during this phase because they feel productive. But those apps rarely expose you to the rhythm, speed, or natural variation of real Spanish. Parrot uses short-form video built on comprehensible input, so daily immersion feels like watching content rather than grinding exercises, with listening practice building alongside spaced-repetition review. Weeks 9 to 12 Communicate, Don't Perform The final month shifts from learning Spanish to using it, a difference that fundamentally changes how progress happens. Why do imperfect sentences build real conversational ability? Long conversations about familiar topics (work, travel, hobbies, family) are the best way to practice. Imperfect sentences aren't mistakes to fix before speaking; they're how you become fluent. Every time you search for a word while talking or rephrase because you can't find the right word, you're building the quick thinking skills that separate real conversation ability from textbook knowledge. What level can you realistically reach in 90 days? Preply's research shows that learners can reach A2 to B1 conversational level in 90 days with structured daily study. This range represents functional ability: ordering food, finding directions, having basic conversations, and understanding podcast content. It's not complete fluency, but it's the foundation for everything else. How does absorbing grammar in context signal a shift to intermediate? Grammar becomes something you notice rather than study from rules. Instead of memorizing verb tables, you observe how native speakers use tenses in interviews or YouTube videos. This shift from studying grammar to acquiring it through context signals a learner's progression from beginner to intermediate. What a Balanced Weekly Routine Actually Looks Like Do four to five structured vocabulary and grammar review sessions of 20 to 30 minutes each. Listen to video or podcast content at your level daily. Have two to three speaking sessions per week through shadowing, self-talk, or conversation exchange. Do one longer immersion session weekly where you consume Spanish purely for enjoyment, without stopping to look things up. Why does the weekly immersion session matter so much? The weekly immersion session trains your brain to handle unclear situations and stay focused despite incomplete understanding. This ability makes real conversations feel manageable instead of overwhelming. What separates learners who finish 90 days with the strongest results? The students who finish 90 days with the strongest results aren't those who studied most in any single week, but those who made the routine small enough to repeat daily and interesting enough that they wanted to. The harder question is whether this goal fits where you are now. Is Three Months the Right Goal for You? Three months is the right goal for most learners , but only if you're honest about what you're measuring . If the target is being able to talk with confidence — having a real conversation , understanding what people say back to you, and continuing without getting stuck — 90 days is absolutely achievable. If the target is professional fluency or native-level precision , three months is a starting point , not a finish line . title: Project-Based Learning for Better AEC Career Outcomes {{year}}
summary: Discover how project-based learning builds practical AEC skills, improves job readiness and supports stronger career outcomes.
body_text: Why is There a Gap Between AEC Education and Industry Expectations The gap between classroom learning and professional practice can be difficult to bridge when learners have limited opportunities to work on realistic AEC challenges. BIM education needs to develop not only technical knowledge but also the BIM skills required to work, communicate and solve problems in project environments. Beyond Software Proficiency: Knowing BIM tools like Revit or Navisworks is only a starting point; BIM professionals also need coordination, problem-solving and information management skills. Limited Project Exposure: Academic exercises may not reflect real project requirements such as multidisciplinary coordination, design changes, clash resolution and documentation. Evolving Industry Workflows: BIM practices continue to develop with cloud collaboration, automation and information management, making industry-relevant learning increasingly important. Applying Skills in Practice: Project-based education allows learners to work through realistic modelling, coordination and documentation tasks, helping them understand how BIM is applied across the project lifecycle. What is Project-Based Learning in AEC Education? Project-based learning in AEC education focuses on learning by working through realistic design and construction challenges rather than relying only on theory. In the AEC industry, learners can use hands-on learning to develop models, coordinate disciplines, review project information and solve practical problems. This approach helps connect classroom concepts with the way professionals work on actual projects. By applying knowledge to project tasks, learners can build technical confidence, improve collaboration and understand how decisions made during design and planning can affect construction outcomes. How Does Project-Based Learning Build Job-ready AEC Skills? Project-based learning helps bridge the gap between classroom knowledge and workplace expectations by giving learners opportunities to practise tasks they may experience on real AEC projects. It strengthens employability skills while making professional training more realistic and relevant. Skill Developed How project-based learning builds it BIM Modelling Learners create and develop discipline-specific models, helping them understand modelling standards, accuracy and project requirements. Coordination Working with different project elements teaches learners how architectural, structural and MEP models need to align within a coordinated workflow. Clash Detection Learners identify conflicts between building systems and explore practical ways to resolve them before they affect construction. Documentation Creating drawings, schedules and model-based deliverables helps learners understand how Building Information Modeling information supports project documentation and communication. Problem-Solving Project tasks require learners to assess issues, consider possible solutions and make informed decisions rather than simply follow instructions. Multidisciplinary Collaboration Working across disciplines develops communication, coordination and teamwork skills that are essential across the AEC industry. Workplace Readiness Completing realistic project tasks helps learners understand professional workflows and apply their technical knowledge with greater confidence. Why Do Real-World AEC Projects Improve BIM Learning? Real-world AEC projects make construction education more meaningful by showing learners how BIM knowledge is used beyond individual tools or classroom exercises. They also help learners understand the practical expectations of BIM jobs. Understand Complete Project Workflows Working through a project helps learners see how information moves from initial design and modelling to coordination, documentation and construction. This gives them a clearer understanding of how different BIM tasks connect. Apply Industry Standards Realistic architectural projects introduce learners to standards, naming conventions, information requirements and documentation practices used to maintain consistency across professional BIM workflows. Connect Design with Construction Project-based tasks can show how design decisions affect coordination, quantities, sequencing and construction. This helps learners understand the link between a digital model and what happens on site. Develop Practical Decision-Making Real projects rarely follow a perfect path. Learners may need to identify clashes, review design changes or choose suitable solutions, helping them develop judgement alongside technical skills. Experience Multidisciplinary Coordination AEC projects involve architects, engineers, contractors and other specialists. Working with different disciplines helps learners understand how information is shared and why coordination matters. Prepare for Workplace Expectations Applying BIM skills to realistic deliverables gives learners experience with the type of tasks, collaboration and problem-solving they may encounter in professional roles. This can make the transition from construction education to BIM employment more confident and practical. How Does Project-Based Learning Strengthen AEC Portfolios and Employability? Project-based learning can make an AEC portfolio more meaningful by showing not just what a learner has studied, but how they can apply their knowledge to realistic project situations. Here are the key ways it can strengthen career development and BIM learning: Build Relevant Project Work: Working on realistic AEC assignments allows learners to create project samples that reflect actual industry workflows, requirements and expected deliverables. Show Practical BIM Skills: Models, drawings, schedules and coordinated outputs can demonstrate how well learners understand BIM tools and apply them to different stages of project development. Demonstrate Problem-Solving: Project-based tasks encourage learners to identify design or coordination issues, assess possible solutions and make decisions based on project requirements. Strengthen Portfolio Quality: An architectural portfolio supported by well-developed projects gives employers a clearer view of a learner’s technical skills, attention to detail and ability to complete practical tasks. Support Career Opportunities: Relevant project evidence can help candidates communicate their capabilities more confidently during job applications, interviews and discussions with potential employers. What Makes an Effective Project-Based AEC Learning Experience? An effective project-based learning experience should reflect how work is actually carried out across the AEC industry. Instead of focusing only on theory, it should give learners opportunities to use construction technology, make decisions and respond to project requirements. Here are some crucial factors that makes project-based learning effective: Realistic project briefs help learners work through challenges similar to those found on professional AEC projects. Mentor feedback helps learners identify mistakes, refine their approach and improve the quality of their work. Team collaboration develops communication, problem-solving, and coordination skills needed when working across AEC disciplines. Industry tools allow learners to practise with BIM software and workflows used in professional environments. Project deliverables give learners tangible outcomes that demonstrate how they can apply their knowledge in practice. How Can Project-Based Learning Prepare You for a BIM Career? Building a BIM career requires more than learning software; professionals also need opportunities to practise workflows, solve project challenges and understand how BIM is used across the AEC industry. For learners who want to turn BIM knowledge into practical workplace skills, Novatr’s BIM Professional Program offers a structured BIM course that connects learning with real AEC project requirements: The seven-month online program covers BIM fundamentals , modelling, documentation, coordination and project delivery through five practical phases. Learners work on project-based learning that helps them apply BIM concepts to realistic project scenarios and develop workplace-ready skills. The program supports different career directions, including AI, automation, project management, sustainability, infrastructure and structural analysis. Learners receive career-focused support through portfolio development, CV and LinkedIn guidance, mock interviews and company-specific assessments. The program is designed for Architects and Civil, Structural, Mechanical and Electrical Engineers, helping them build relevant BIM capabilities for evolving AEC roles.

Why it stands out Uses micro-fine Zinc Oxide and Centella Asiatica for chemical-free defense. How to use Apply evenly to lips 15 minutes before sun exposure. How to Choose the Lip Balm for Men? There are numerous choices available in the market, and the best one depends on your individual lip issues, skin type, and routine. Before purchasing, here's what to keep in mind before you buy: Identify concern first : Different balms have different uses so you want to find one that will deal with dryness, darkness, cracking, or sun exposure. SPF : Look for SPF protection if you spend a lot of time in the sun and/or often ride a bike or motorcycle. Fragrance Check: Look for a fragrance-free or mild formula if you have sensitive skin as strong fragrances can sometimes cause irritation over time. Texture: Pick a texture you'll actually use. Sticks are handy for use when on the go, and pots or tubes are great for the bedtime routine. Consider tinted or non-tinted options: A tinted lip balm for men can help even out lip tone subtly without looking like makeup. Read the ingredient list: Look at the list of ingredients. Opt for natural moisturisers and stay away from chemical compounds that will further dry lips with repeated use. Lip Problems Men Commonly Face Men experience a fairly specific set of lip concerns, often linked to lifestyle habits and lower awareness around lip care. Understanding these problems makes it easier to pick a targeted solution. Chapped and Cracked Lips: They dry out from frequent exposure to sun, wind and dry air resulting in cracks and flaking that are clearly visible. Dark or Pigmented Lips : Lips can become discolored over time due to smoking, excessive caffeine, sun exposure, and a lack of water. Dry, Flaky Skin: When moisturisation is not done regularly, it can lead to a rough and flaky appearance, which can be uncomfortable and unattractive. Chronic Lip Dryness: Some men deal with persistently dry lips regardless of the season, often due to dehydration or certain medications. Sunburned Lips: The tender skin on the lips can be damaged by the sun, resulting in redness, peeling and sensitivity. Cracked Corners of the Mouth: Also known as angular cheilitis, this happens due to a mix of dryness, saliva buildup, or nutritional deficiencies. What Ingredients Should Men Look for in a Lip Balm? Choosing a lip balm with the right ingredients can make the difference between a product that truly heals your lips and one that offers only temporary relief. Here's what to look for on the label. Shea Butter: Deeply moisturising and rich in fatty acids, shea butter helps repair dry, cracked lips effectively. Beeswax: This natural ingredient forms a protective barrier on the lips, locking in moisture and shielding against environmental damage. Vitamin E : A powerful antioxidant, vitamin E helps nourish the skin and supports the repair of damaged lip tissue. Coconut Oil: Lightweight yet hydrating, coconut oil soothes dryness and adds a natural softness to the lips. SPF (Sun Protection Factor): Balms with SPF protect against UV-induced darkening and long-term sun damage. Natural Brightening Agents: Ingredients like vitamin C, licorice extract, or niacinamide can help with lip balm for dark lips concerns by gradually evening out pigmentation. Ingredients to Avoid in Lip Balms Many ingredients in lip balms may even cause dryness or irritate sensitive lip skin over time. There are some ingredients which are not recommended for lips: Menthol and Camphor: While they create a cooling sensation, these ingredients can be drying and may lead to a cycle of dependency on the balm. Salicylic Acid: Commonly used in exfoliants, this can be too harsh and drying for the delicate lip area. Synthetic Fragrances: Artificial scents can trigger irritation or allergic reactions in sensitive individuals. Phenol: This ingredient can be extremely drying and irritating with regular use, despite offering short-term relief. Alcohol: Denatured or drying alcohols strip natural moisture and can worsen chapped lips instead of healing them. Artificial Colours and Dyes: These offer no real skincare benefit and can sometimes cause sensitivity in certain individuals. Application Tips to Use a Lip Balm in the Correct Way Morning Apply lip balm after brushing your teeth. Apply it after washing your face. Select a lip balm that contains SPF if you are heading out. It will help to maintain healthy lips all through the day. Throughout the Day Keep reapplying lip balm every few hours. Reapply after eating or drinking. Apply more frequently in air-conditioned environments. Reapply after being out in windy conditions. Regular application helps keep lips soft and hydrated. Night Apply lip balm before bedtime. Apply a thicker lip balm at night. Cover the lips evenly with a generous layer. Leave it overnight to help prevent dryness and support lip recovery. Common Lip Care Mistakes Men Should Avoid Even with a good lip balm in hand, small habits can undo its benefits. Here are mistakes to watch out for. Licking Your Lips Frequently: Saliva evaporates quickly and actually dries out the lips further, worsening chapping over time. Skipping SPF: Ignoring sun protection accelerates darkening and long-term damage to lip skin. Using Expired Products: Old or expired balms can lose effectiveness and may irritate the lips. Over-Exfoliating: Scrubbing lips too often or too harshly can cause micro-tears and increased sensitivity. Not Staying Hydrated: Drinking too little water shows up first on the lips, making them dry and prone to cracking. Choosing the Wrong Formula: Using a balm not suited to your specific concern, such as picking a plain hydrating stick when you actually need a men's lip balm for dark lips, delays results. Final Thoughts Taking care of the lips is definitely not a winter-only it should be a part of a man's daily routine. The difference between the best lip balm for dry lips can rely on daily and a tinted lip balm with a natural tinting is only due to their choice of product and the correct application schedule. Be mindful of ingredients, and avoid the common mistakes listed above and then select the right formula for your particular lip needs. In just the right routine, smoother, healthier and even toned lips are closer than you think.

title: Microschool vs. Traditional School: What Actually Changes for Your Child (2026)
summary: If you're comparing a microschool to your child's current school, you're probably carrying a quieter worry under all the logistics. Am I really making the right call for my child? A lot of families are sitting with that exact question right now, and feeling unsure about it is completely normal. Neither option is better than A look at how microschool and traditional school differ in class size, pace, schedule, and community, and how to tell which one fits your child.
body_text: If you’re comparing a microschool to your child’s current school, you’re probably carrying a quieter worry under all the logistics. Am I really making the right call for my child? A lot of families are sitting with that exact question right now, and feeling unsure about it is completely normal. Neither option is better than the other. A traditional school and a microschool are built to do different things. A traditional school is designed to teach a lot of children well at once. A microschool is built around a much smaller group, with room to bend to one child. So the real question isn’t which model is better, it’s which one is right for your child. We’re KaiPod Learning, and we work alongside more than 150 microschool founders across 30+ states. Because we see so many schools up close, we can tell you what microschools are actually like day to day. And when you’re ready, you can use our free Microschool Directory to find options near you. Below, we walk through the handful of differences that matter most, so you can picture both options clearly. What do we mean by “traditional school”? When we say traditional school, we mean the kind most children attend, whether that’s public, private, charter, or parochial. They differ in funding, governance, and culture, but the basic setup is the same. Children are grouped by age, move through a fixed schedule and a set curriculum, and learn in larger classes, commonly around 20 to 25 students with one teacher. So if your child is in a private or parochial school and “traditional” doesn’t feel like your word, this is still for you. What we’re really comparing is the shape of your child’s day, the same-age classroom, the set schedule, and the one pace the whole group moves at. What is a microschool? A microschool is a small, mixed-age learning community where the teaching is built around each child. The whole school is usually small, with one or two educators, so the group your child is part of tends to stay around 10 to 15 children at a time. Most of the difference comes from the small class size. If you want the fuller picture, our posts on what a microschool is and how microschools work go deeper. And if you’re wondering whether “microschool” just means homeschooling, it’s not. Our post on the key differences between microschooling and homeschooling breaks down why. Day-in-the-life differences Only a handful of things really change what a child’s day feels like from morning to afternoon. Here they are side by side, and then we’ll go through what each one means for your child. What changes Microschool Traditional school Class size Usually 10 to 15 children, with one or two educators Commonly around 20 to 25 students with one teacher Personalization and pace Personalized; your child moves at their own pace, often with project-based work A shared, grade-level curriculum and pace for the whole class Schedule Varies by school; full-time, part-time, and hybrid schedules are common A fixed, full-time schedule, usually five days a week Learning environment A small, mixed-age community Age-graded classrooms with a larger peer group Class size and relationships In a smaller group, your child is easy for an educator to notice, without being put on the spot. Imagine a child who tends to go quiet in a big classroom, hoping no one calls on them, or one who needs a teacher to check in before diving into something hard. In a group of ten or twelve, that check-in happens naturally, without singling anyone out in front of the room. For a child like that, just being seen without being spotlighted can change how the whole day feels. The average public school class runs around 20 students , with one teacher keeping the whole room on track at once. Therefore, the teaching has to aim for the middle of the class. In a smaller group, the educator actually has room to notice what your child needs on a given day and respond to it. In a 2025 EdChoice survey of families in one microschool network, 86% said they were very or extremely confident in their educator’s ability to help their child succeed. None of this means a big class is a bad class. Plenty of children do beautifully in a busy room and love the energy of a large peer group. It comes down to what your child needs to feel settled enough to learn. Pace The work meets your child where they actually are, instead of where the calendar says they should be. A child who needs an extra week on fractions can take it, instead of being left behind when the class moves on. A child who already understands the concepts doesn’t have to sit and wait, quietly growing bored. The same child often needs both, faster in one subject and slower in another. A traditional class has to keep moving to get through the year’s curriculum before testing. That’s efficient, but a child who fell behind in week three can pile up gaps, while a child who’s ahead gets restless. A microschool does it the other way around, holding the learning steady and letting the time stretch or shrink to fit. There’s research behind this, too. A RAND Corporation evaluation found that tailoring the pace and focus of instruction to each student can improve achievement no matter where a child starts. Pace is about how your child moves through material. The schedule is about when school happens, which is a separate thing that matters to different families. We’ll take that next. Schedule Microschools often run more than one schedule. You might choose a full five-day week, or a lighter, more concentrated schedule that keeps more of the week open. If your child struggles to make it through a full seven-hour day, a lighter schedule may work better for them. A traditional school runs a fixed, full-time day and calendar. That predictability is a big part of what makes it so dependable for working families, and it’s a real strength. Microschools tend to be more flexible. In the National Microschooling Center’s 2026 sector analysis , which surveyed 1,000 microschools across all fifty states, 64% ran a full-time weekly schedule, while 30% ran part-time or hybrid schedules and 17% offered families both options. A flexible schedule is one of the most common reasons families start looking at microschools in the first place. Learning environment Instead of a roomful of children the same age, your child is part of a small, mixed-age group. The older children grow into mentors, which builds their confidence and sense of responsibility, and the younger ones stretch by watching and working next to them. When everyone’s working on something a little different, the pressure to be exactly “on grade level” eases for every child. Traditional schools group children strictly by age, which works well for teaching one grade’s material and gives a child a big group of same-age friends to grow up with. In a microschool, the small size makes a mixed-age group the natural setup, and because it’s small, children are simply more visible, to each other and to the adults. Picture your child spending one week getting help from an older student on a tricky reading passage, and the next week explaining a math step to someone younger. That back-and-forth is just what a mixed-age room feels like day to day. So which one fits better? There’s no single answer that fits every child, and that’s okay. Some children do best with the structure, the predictability, and the big peer group of a traditional school. Others really come into their own when the group is small and the pace and schedule meets their needs. If you’re trying to figure out where your own child fits, our roadmap for families thinking about switching schools is a good next read. If you’re further along and want the nitty-gritty, things like progress tracking, transcripts, accreditation, and how your child will make friends, that’s covered in our posts on the pros and cons of microschools . And when you’re ready to go deeper, our 2026 Family Guide to Microschools walks you through the rest, with worksheets, checklists, and a closer look at how to decide. You may be interested in What Is a Microschool? How Do Microschools Work? Reasons to Switch Schools 10 Key Differences Between Microschooling and Homeschooling
